newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's new leftist government drafts wish-list.
newsitem.headline: France's new leftist government drafts wish-list.

text.p: France's new leftist government, fresh from its first cabinet meeting with conservative President Jacques Chirac, is compiling a list of tasks and priorities for Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, a spokeswoman said.
"The prime minister will make a declaration of general policy and announce his calendar and priorities in a few days," said government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann.

"At the present time, the various members of the government are drafting lists of urgent tasks and at the same time lists of what should be proposed to the prime minister as new priorities. So this matter is going forward progressively."

Jospin, on his first official international trip, chatted briefly with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair about the difficulties facing the European Union's plans for European monetary union, according to a British official.
"They both spoke of the difficulties the single currency would face," said the official, without offering details.
Jospin and Blair were both in Malmo, Sweden, for a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties from Europe. Jospin was to address the conference and hold more talks with Blair on Friday.

Members of France's new leftist cabinet fanned out across Paris on Thursday to take over their respective ministries in a series of ceremonies marking the formal transition of power from the centre-right government defeated in last Sunday's elections.
The 26-strong cabinet includes several women in senior posts, the first Communist ministers since 1984 and a Green minister of the environment.
After just one day in office, Trautmann said, "our team is ready to work, drawn together, motivated, enthusiastic."
The buoyuant ministers gathered at the Elysee presidential palace on Thursday morning for an initial meeting with a grim-faced Chirac.
"Here we are in a new period of 'cohabitation'," Chirac said, using the French term for power-sharing between a government and president of different political persuasions.
It is the third period of cohabitation in the history of France's Fifth Republic, set up in 1958, but the first between a left-wing prime minister and a right-wing head of state.
Jospin said the 30-minute meeting launching power-sharing went "well, very well." He said the tone was serious but relaxed.

The Paris Bourse saluted the broadly pro-European government, in which Communists hostile to a European single currency were confined to the transport and sports ministries, and the CAC-40 stock index gained 2.11 percent for the day.
New Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou said her most urgent task would be to restore confidence in the independence of the judicial system.
Judges have already opened several investigations into politically-charged cases involving alleged illicit party funding, rigged public tenders and illegal bugging.

Chirac's disastrous gamble in calling National Assembly elections 10 months ahead of schedule, only to lose the centre-right's huge majority in parliament, has left his Gaullist RPR party in deep disarray.

Former parliamentary speaker Philippe Seguin, who led the 1992 campaign in France against the Maastricht treaty on European economic and monetary union, formally announced his candidacy to succeed defeated prime minister Alain Juppe as RPR leader.
Senior Gaullist Charles Pasqua, a Seguin supporter, said there was broad consensus for holding a special party congress on July 5 at which a new leader would be chosen.
